q: A startup wants to launch quickly with minimal infrastructure management, but portability to another cloud provider later matters more to them than convenience today. Which service model best serves that stated priority?
opts: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
A Reserved Instance commitment on a single VM family
why: IaaS resources like VMs are the most portable between providers, since they're closer to raw infrastructure. PaaS launches faster but leans on provider-specific platform features that make leaving harder — a real trade-off, and the question asks which priority wins. A Reserved Instance is a pricing commitment, not a service model, and doesn't address portability at all.

q: A finance team complains their monthly Azure bill is unpredictable and spikes randomly, even though nothing about their workload has changed. Which cloud characteristic is failing here?
opts: High availability
Predictability
Scalability
Elasticity
why: Predictability is about consistent, forecastable cost and performance — an erratic bill with unchanged usage signals this isn't being managed well. Scalability, availability, and elasticity all describe how resources respond to load, not billing consistency.

q: An operations team manually adds two web servers the day before a product launch and removes them a week later. A colleague describes this as 'the app's elasticity at work.' Which term correctly describes what happened?
opts: Scalability but not elasticity, because the change was planned and manual
Elasticity, because capacity both increased and later decreased again
Neither, because only automatic changes count as scaling at all
Elasticity for the scale-out step, and scalability for the later scale-in
why: Scalability is the general ability to handle more load by adding resources, whether a human does it or not — which is exactly what this team did. Elasticity is the narrower, automatic form: capacity grows and shrinks in response to real-time demand without an administrator planning it. Growing and shrinking is not enough to make it elastic if each step was manual; manual changes still count as scaling; and the direction of the change (out versus in) has nothing to do with which term applies.

q: A company currently spends heavily on capital equipment refreshes every three years for its datacenter. Moving fully to Azure IaaS would primarily shift this spending pattern to:
opts: A one-time Reserved Instance prepayment classified as CapEx
OpEx
A smaller but still recurring CapEx
No change in spending pattern
why: Cloud computing shifts organizations from large upfront capital purchases toward ongoing operating expense. Even a Reserved Instance paid upfront is a discounted commitment to consume Azure capacity, not the purchase of equipment the company owns, so it is not CapEx in the datacenter sense, a commonly missed distinction.

q: Which of these best illustrates the shared responsibility model shifting MORE responsibility to Microsoft, compared with a self-managed deployment?
opts: Moving a file server to an Azure VM running the same OS as before
Assigning an additional RBAC role to the team managing a self-managed VM
Enabling a Read-only resource lock on a self-managed VM
Moving a database to Azure SQL Database (PaaS) instead of a self-managed SQL Server on a VM
why: PaaS services like Azure SQL Database hand OS patching and infrastructure management to Microsoft, shifting more of the split toward the provider than a lift-and-shift VM does. A resource lock or an RBAC assignment changes who on your team can do what — it doesn't move any responsibility to Microsoft at all.

q: A team wants to run a low-priority batch job at the lowest possible cost, and can tolerate the job being interrupted and restarted if Azure needs the capacity back. Which pricing approach fits?
opts: Standard pay-as-you-go pricing
Reserved instances
Spot pricing
An Azure Savings Plan for compute
why: Spot pricing offers deep discounts in exchange for the possibility of eviction with little notice — ideal for interruption-tolerant, low-priority work. Reserved instances and Savings Plans both trade a usage commitment for a discount, but neither involves eviction risk, so neither passes on the deepest possible discount this scenario allows for.

q: A company uses Microsoft 365 for email, Azure App Service for its website, and SQL Server installed on an Azure virtual machine. A new hire claims the company 'uses no IaaS at all.' Which correction is accurate?
opts: The SQL Server VM is IaaS; App Service is PaaS and Microsoft 365 is SaaS
App Service is IaaS, because the company deploys its own code to it
Microsoft 365 is IaaS, because it runs on infrastructure Microsoft owns
Both App Service and the VM are IaaS, since both host company workloads
why: Installing SQL Server on a VM means the company manages the guest OS and everything above it — the defining trait of IaaS. App Service is PaaS: deploying your own code to a managed runtime is what PaaS is for, not a sign of IaaS. Microsoft 365 is a finished application the company only consumes (SaaS); the fact that it runs on Microsoft-owned hardware is true of every cloud model and doesn't make it IaaS. Hosting a workload isn't the test either — what matters is which layers the customer manages.

q: A retailer's site traffic multiplies 10x during a single holiday weekend, then returns to normal a few days later. Which cloud characteristic most directly and cost-effectively addresses this, as opposed to simply over-provisioning fixed capacity year-round?
opts: Zero Trust
Elasticity
Availability sets
Reserved Instances
why: Elasticity lets resources scale up automatically for the surge and back down afterward, avoiding paying for peak capacity year-round. Availability sets protect against hardware failure, not demand spikes, and Reserved Instances lock in a fixed commitment — the opposite of what a short, unpredictable spike calls for.

q: Why might an organization choose a hybrid cloud model even though it's more complex to manage than pure public cloud?
opts: Hybrid deployments typically cost less overall than pure public cloud once egress and support fees are added in
Moving fully to public cloud removes the need to manage identity for any on-premises systems that remain
Regulatory or data residency requirements may require some data to stay on-premises
Azure's regional footprint covers most countries, which usually removes data residency as a reason to go hybrid
why: Compliance and data residency needs are a common, legitimate reason to keep some workloads on-premises while using public cloud elsewhere — some regulations specifically require certain data to stay off public cloud infrastructure entirely, not just within a given country's borders. Hybrid isn't reliably cheaper once you factor in running two environments, and identity still has to be managed for whatever on-premises systems remain, typically unified with something like Microsoft Entra ID rather than eliminated.

q: A finance department wants to compare five years of projected on-premises costs against five years of projected Azure costs before deciding whether to migrate at all. Which tool fits?
opts: Azure Advisor
The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator
The Azure Pricing calculator
Azure Cost Management
why: The TCO calculator is built specifically to compare projected on-premises cost against projected Azure cost before a migration decision. The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of specific Azure resources you already plan to deploy, and Cost Management/Advisor both analyze spend on resources you already have running — none of the other three compare against an on-premises baseline.

q: A CIO's migration business case lists four expected benefits of moving to Azure. Which one should be removed because it misstates how Azure works?
opts: Capacity can be added in minutes without a hardware procurement cycle
Spreading a workload across availability zones can raise its availability
Microsoft takes over securing the company's data and user identities
Compute can automatically scale down during low-demand periods
why: Under the shared responsibility model the customer always keeps responsibility for their own data, identities, and access, in every service model — so this line in the business case is simply wrong. The other three are genuine, well-documented benefits: agility (provisioning in minutes), high availability (zone-redundant deployment), and elasticity (automatic scale-down). Each of those is phrased with a hedge ('can'), which is exactly how a realistic benefit statement should read.

q: A company wants to avoid vendor lock-in as much as possible while still gaining cloud cost savings. Which general guidance is most accurate?
opts: Signing a Reserved Instance commitment is what creates vendor lock-in, not the service model chosen
IaaS workloads are generally easier to move between providers than deeply-integrated PaaS/SaaS workloads, though some lock-in risk always exists
Lock-in risk is the same across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, since all three run on Microsoft-owned datacenters
Choosing PaaS over IaaS whenever possible minimizes lock-in, since PaaS abstracts away the underlying infrastructure
why: IaaS resources are closer to raw infrastructure and generally port more easily than workloads built around a provider's specific PaaS or SaaS features. PaaS abstracting the infrastructure is exactly what deepens lock-in, not what reduces it, and lock-in risk very much differs by service model — a Reserved Instance is a pricing choice with no bearing on portability.

q: In a PaaS deployment such as Azure SQL Database, responsibility for classifying the data and deciding who may access it transfers to Microsoft.
opts: True
False
why: Moving to PaaS hands Microsoft the operating system, database engine patching, and the underlying infrastructure — but data classification, identities, and access decisions stay with the customer in every service model, including SaaS. The misconception this statement encodes is that 'more managed' eventually means 'Microsoft owns the data responsibility'; the shared responsibility model never reaches that point.

q: A virtual machine that has been stopped (deallocated) from the Azure portal continues to accrue compute charges until it is deleted.
opts: True
False
why: Under the consumption-based model, a deallocated VM releases its compute capacity and stops incurring compute charges; only its disks and any reserved public IP keep billing. The trap is the difference between stopping from the portal (deallocated, not billed for compute) and shutting down from inside the guest OS (still allocated, still billed) — the exam expects you to know that 'stopped' alone does not guarantee savings.

q: In a PaaS service such as Azure App Service, the customer chooses when security patches are applied to the underlying guest operating system.
opts: True
False
why: Giving up control of the OS is the defining trade of PaaS: Microsoft patches the operating system and runtime on its own schedule, and in exchange the customer manages only the application and its data. A team that needs to control patch timing — for example to satisfy an audit window — needs IaaS, where the guest OS is theirs to patch. The statement describes IaaS-level control and misattributes it to PaaS.

q: An Azure Functions app on the Consumption plan incurs compute charges continuously while it is deployed, even during hours in which no executions occur.
opts: True
False
why: Serverless billing is tied to execution: on the Consumption plan you pay per execution and for the compute consumed while code runs, and a function that is deployed but idle costs nothing in compute (its storage account still bills a small amount). This is what distinguishes serverless from a VM or an always-on App Service plan, which bill for provisioned capacity whether or not it is used. The statement applies the provisioned-capacity model to serverless, which is exactly the misconception the exam checks.

q: Manually resizing a virtual machine from a D2 to a D4 size the night before a planned product launch is an example of elasticity.
opts: True
False
why: This is vertical scaling performed by hand — a legitimate example of scalability, since capacity was added to handle more load. Elasticity specifically means capacity expands and contracts automatically in response to real-time demand, with no administrator scheduling the change. A planned, manual resize fails the 'automatic' test, so calling it elasticity is the error the exam is probing for.

q: Lifting-and-shifting on-premises servers to equivalently sized Azure VMs that run 24 hours a day captures the cloud's cost advantage on its own, because the billing is consumption-based.
opts: True
False
why: Consumption-based billing only saves money when consumption actually drops — by deallocating idle VMs, right-sizing, autoscaling, or moving to PaaS or serverless where appropriate. A like-for-like migration of always-on, fixed-size VMs reproduces the on-premises usage pattern in the cloud and can easily cost more than the hardware it replaced. The misconception here is treating pay-as-you-go as a discount in itself rather than an opportunity that still has to be exploited.

q: Setting a Spot virtual machine's maximum price equal to the regular pay-as-you-go rate guarantees that Azure will never evict it.
opts: True
False
why: A Spot VM can be evicted for two reasons: the Spot price rising above your maximum, or Azure needing the capacity back. Setting the maximum price to the pay-as-you-go rate removes the first reason but not the second — a capacity-driven eviction can still happen with little notice at any price. That is why Spot is only suitable for interruption-tolerant work regardless of how the price cap is set, which is the point this statement gets wrong.

q: A team is listing which parts of its proposed Azure design will never require them to patch an operating system. Which two services in the design meet that bar? (Choose two.)
opts: Azure SQL Database
SQL Server installed on an Azure virtual machine
Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts
why: Azure SQL Database and App Service are PaaS: Microsoft owns the operating system and runtime patching, and the team manages only data and code. SQL Server on a VM is the near-miss — it is the same database engine, but running on IaaS, so the guest OS (and the engine itself) are the customer's to patch. Azure Virtual Desktop is a managed service for the brokering and gateway layer, but its session hosts are VMs in the customer's subscription whose Windows OS the customer still patches.

q: A CTO drafts five expected outcomes of moving a line-of-business app to Azure. Which two are realistic expectations? (Choose two.)
opts: Extra capacity can be added within minutes rather than after a procurement cycle
Microsoft assumes responsibility for classifying and protecting the company's data
Deploying across availability zones can raise availability beyond a single datacenter
The monthly bill becomes fixed and predictable regardless of how much is used
The service SLA guarantees the app will experience zero downtime
why: Agility (provisioning in minutes) and higher availability through zone-redundant deployment are genuine, documented benefits. The other three each encode a common misconception: data classification and protection stay with the customer under the shared responsibility model; consumption-based billing makes cost track usage, which is the opposite of fixed — predictability comes from managing it, not from the model itself; and an SLA is a commitment with service credits for missed targets, never a zero-downtime guarantee.

q: A development VM is only used during office hours but currently costs the same every month. Which two actions would actually reduce its compute charges under Azure's consumption-based model? (Choose two.)
opts: Deallocate the VM from the portal each evening and start it each morning
Shut the VM down from inside the guest operating system each evening
Resize it to a smaller VM size that still handles the daytime load
Apply a Delete lock so it cannot be removed accidentally
Add a CostCenter tag so the charge appears under the development team
why: Compute is billed while a VM is allocated, so deallocating it (portal stop, auto-shutdown, or CLI) removes roughly two-thirds of the hours from the bill, and a smaller size lowers the hourly rate for the hours that remain. The near-miss is shutting down from inside the OS: the VM stops but stays allocated, so Azure keeps charging for the reserved compute. A Delete lock protects the resource and a tag changes how the charge is reported — neither reduces what is consumed.

q: A company runs SQL Server on an Azure VM (IaaS) and also uses Azure SQL Database (PaaS). Which two responsibilities belong to the company in BOTH deployments? (Choose two.)
opts: Classifying the data stored in each database
Managing the accounts and identities that may access each database
Patching the database engine
Physical security of the datacenter hardware
Patching the guest operating system
why: Data classification and identity and access management never leave the customer, whatever the service model — that is the fixed core of the shared responsibility model. The other three split by model: engine and guest-OS patching are the customer's job on the IaaS VM but Microsoft's job for Azure SQL Database, so neither is shared across both deployments, and physical datacenter security is always Microsoft's. Picking 'patching' is the typical error: it is true for one of the two deployments, not both.

q: An organization intentionally runs some workloads in Azure and others in a different public cloud provider, specifically to avoid depending on one vendor and to use whichever provider's service is strongest for a given need. Which deployment model does this describe?
opts: Private cloud
Multi-cloud
Hybrid cloud
A single Azure region deployment with availability zones
why: Multi-cloud specifically means deliberately using more than one public cloud provider. Hybrid cloud instead combines on-premises/private infrastructure with public cloud — a different axis entirely. Private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, and availability zones are a within-region resilience feature, unrelated to which providers are in use.

q: A feature in Public preview in Azure always carries the exact same SLA guarantee as a Generally Available (GA) feature.
opts: True
False
why: Preview features are commonly excluded from SLA guarantees and may still change before reaching General Availability — the full committed SLA applies once a feature is GA.

q: A startup wants to be able to spin up a new test environment in minutes rather than the weeks a traditional hardware procurement process would take, so they can experiment and iterate faster. Which cloud benefit does this best describe?
opts: Agility
Elasticity
High availability
A composite SLA
why: Agility describes the speed at which new resources can be provisioned and iterated on, cutting procurement time from weeks to minutes. Elasticity is specifically about automatically scaling existing resources up and down with real-time demand, not the initial speed of provisioning something new. High availability and composite SLA both describe uptime characteristics, not provisioning speed.

q: A payment system is designed so that if one of its redundant application servers crashes, traffic fails over to a healthy server so fast that users notice zero interruption at all. Which term most precisely describes this specific quality?
opts: High availability
Disaster recovery
Scalability
Fault tolerance
why: Fault tolerance describes a system that keeps running with no perceptible interruption even when a component fails outright — the instant, seamless failover described here. High availability is the broader goal of staying up a very high percentage of the time, which can tolerate a brief blip during failover; fault tolerance is the stricter, zero-interruption version of that idea. Disaster recovery is the process of restoring service after a major outage has already happened, and scalability is about handling more load, not surviving a component failure.

q: Because Azure aggregates compute and storage demand across millions of customers in large-scale datacenters, it can typically achieve a lower per-unit infrastructure cost than most individual organizations running their own private datacenter.
opts: True
False
why: This is the economies-of-scale argument behind cloud pricing: pooling massive aggregate demand lets a provider buy hardware and power at a scale, and utilization rate, that a single organization's own datacenter usually cannot match, which is part of why cloud compute is often cheaper per unit than self-owned infrastructure of the same capacity. It doesn't mean cloud spending is automatically lower in every case — usage patterns still matter — but the underlying cost structure genuinely favors the aggregated, large-scale provider.

q: A company moves its servers from its own building into a rented colocation facility but keeps buying and refreshing the hardware itself. The CFO says this completes the same CapEx-to-OpEx shift the cloud would deliver. Which assessment is accurate?
opts: Facility costs become OpEx, but the hardware purchases remain CapEx
It is the full CapEx-to-OpEx shift, equivalent to moving to Azure
It is a move from OpEx to CapEx, since the lease is a long-term commitment
Nothing changes, because colocation is a form of private cloud
why: Renting rack space turns the building and power into an ongoing operating expense, but every server refresh is still a large upfront capital purchase — the hardware is still owned. The cloud shift goes further because compute itself is consumed and billed as OpEx, with no equipment to buy. A lease is an OpEx commitment, not CapEx, so calling this a move from OpEx to CapEx has the direction backwards, and even if the arrangement were called a private cloud, the spending pattern has still partly changed, so 'nothing changes' is wrong too.

q: A media company's video transcoding workload runs only when a customer uploads a new file, with uploads arriving at unpredictable times throughout the day. Which combination of characteristics would let them avoid paying for idle compute between uploads?
opts: Elasticity combined with a consumption-based pricing model
High availability combined with a Reserved Instance commitment
Predictability combined with a fixed capacity reservation
Redundancy combined with a three-year Savings Plan
why: Elasticity lets compute scale down to nothing between uploads, and consumption-based pricing means they're billed only for compute actually used — together, no charge accrues while idle. A Reserved Instance or Savings Plan both commit to paying for capacity whether or not it's used, and neither high availability nor redundancy addresses idle-time cost at all.

q: A regulated financial firm wants to modernize an aging application. They need to keep full control over OS-level security patching schedules for audit reasons, but also want Microsoft to manage the underlying physical hardware and virtualization layer. Which service model best fits, and why don't PaaS or SaaS work here?
opts: IaaS, because PaaS and SaaS both hand OS patching to Microsoft, removing the firm's ability to control that schedule
PaaS, because it lets the firm choose its own patching schedule while Microsoft still manages hardware
SaaS, because it gives the firm the most granular control over the operating system
IaaS, because Microsoft delegates hardware management to the customer once they take on OS patching duties
why: IaaS leaves OS-level patching in the customer's hands while Microsoft still manages the physical hardware and virtualization layer beneath it — matching both stated requirements. PaaS abstracts away OS management (the firm couldn't control its own patch schedule), SaaS gives essentially no infrastructure control at all, and the claim that Microsoft hands hardware management to the customer has the IaaS division backwards: Microsoft keeps managing the physical hardware in IaaS regardless of who patches the OS.

q: A company runs several hundred VMs on VMware in a private datacenter whose lease ends in six months. The team wants to run those same VMware workloads in Azure without re-platforming each VM or retraining administrators. Which Azure offering is designed for this?
opts: Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure Data Box
Azure VMware Solution
why: Azure VMware Solution lets an organization already established on VMware run those workloads in Azure with integration and scalability, which is the stated goal. Azure Arc-enabled servers is the near miss: it projects machines into Azure for governance and management but leaves them running where they are rather than moving them. Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops and apps, and Azure Data Box is a physical device for moving large amounts of data, not for running VMs.

q: A VM running an in-memory database is running out of memory, and the team doubles the RAM by resizing the VM to a larger size. Meanwhile, a separate web tier is handled by adding six identical VMs behind a load balancer during peaks. Which pairing correctly names these two approaches?
opts: The resize is horizontal scaling and the extra VMs are vertical scaling
The resize is vertical scaling and the extra VMs are horizontal scaling
Both are horizontal scaling because both add capacity
Both are vertical scaling because both involve virtual machines
why: Vertical scaling changes the capability of an existing resource, such as adding RAM or CPU by moving to a bigger size, while horizontal scaling changes how many resources there are by adding or removing instances. The first pairing reverses the terms. Treating both as the same type ignores the difference the scenario is built around: one changes the size of a single machine, the other the number of machines.

q: Which statement about the Azure free account (free trial subscription) is accurate?
opts: It includes credit to spend within the first 30 days, some products free for 12 months, and more than 25 always-free products
The included credit can be spent at any time during the first 12 months of the subscription
Every Azure service is free for the first 12 months, and the credit never expires
Usage beyond the free allowances is blocked until the owner explicitly chooses a paid plan
why: The free subscription combines three things: credit to spend within the first 30 days, a set of products that are free for 12 months, and more than 25 products that are always free, subject to availability. It does not make every service free, and the credit does not stretch across the year. Usage beyond the free amounts is not simply blocked; it is charged at normal rates once the credit is gone or the free period ends.

q: In a SaaS deployment such as Microsoft 365, the customer remains responsible for the accounts and identities of its users and for the devices allowed to connect.
opts: True
False
why: Whatever the service type, the customer keeps responsibility for its data, the devices that connect, and the identities of people, services, and devices, while the provider always owns the physical datacenter, network, and hosts. SaaS shifts the most to the provider, but not these three.

q: The credit included with an Azure free trial subscription can be spent at any point during its first 12 months.
opts: True
False
why: The credit must be spent within the first 30 days. The 12-month benefit applies to a specific set of products that are free for 12 months, alongside more than 25 products that are always free. Confusing the two periods is the common mistake.

q: Which two actions are examples of vertical scaling? (Choose two.)
opts: Resizing a database VM from 16 GB of RAM to 64 GB
Adding four identical VMs to a scale set before a sale
Moving a VM from a 2-vCPU size to an 8-vCPU size
Adding more containers to a deployment as traffic grows
why: Vertical scaling changes the capability of an existing resource, such as adding RAM or CPU by moving to a bigger size. Adding VMs to a scale set or containers to a deployment changes the number of resources, which is horizontal scaling, specifically scaling out.

q: Which two statements about security and governance benefits in the cloud are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Templates help ensure deployed resources meet technical and regulatory standards, and can be updated at scale when standards change
Cloud-based auditing can flag resources that are out of compliance with a baseline and suggest mitigation
Moving to the cloud moves all OS patching to the provider in every service model
Because providers absorb DDoS attacks well, customers no longer need to manage user identities
why: Templates and auditing are both governance benefits Microsoft describes. Patching is the near miss: on IaaS the customer still patches the guest OS, and only PaaS and SaaS shift most of that work to the provider. Identity management always stays with the customer, regardless of how well the provider handles network attacks.

q: A company has Dev, Test, and Prod subscriptions and wants one policy requiring 'US regions only' applied consistently across all three, without configuring it three separate times or affecting other subscriptions outside this company's tenant. Where should it be assigned?
opts: At the tenant root management group, since policy can only be scoped to an entire tenant
At each resource group individually, since policy cannot be assigned above the resource group level
Only through RBAC role assignments on each subscription
At a management group containing exactly these three subscriptions
why: Management groups let you assign governance once and have it flow down to every subscription beneath them — creating one scoped to just these three subscriptions avoids configuring it three times AND avoids affecting anything outside that group. The tenant root group would work but is broader than needed; policy can absolutely be scoped above the resource group level; and RBAC controls permissions, not configuration rules like allowed regions.

q: A team needs compute for a task that runs unpredictably, roughly twice a month, triggered by an uploaded file, and finishes in under 10 minutes each time. Which is the most cost-effective choice?
opts: A single reserved-capacity VM instance
A VM Scale Set with a fixed minimum of 5 instances
Azure Functions (serverless)
A permanently running virtual machine
why: Serverless Functions only bill for actual execution time, making them far more cost-effective than infrastructure that runs constantly for a task that fires a couple of times a month. A Scale Set with a fixed minimum still keeps 5 instances running at all times, and reserving capacity commits to paying for a VM whether or not the trigger ever fires.

q: A company needs its on-premises network connected to Azure with predictable, low latency, avoiding the public internet entirely, for a latency-sensitive workload. Which service fits best?
opts: VPN Gateway
A Virtual WAN hub connecting sites over the internet
Azure Front Door
ExpressRoute
why: ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection that doesn't traverse the public internet, giving the most predictable latency of the options here. VPN Gateway and an internet-based Virtual WAN hub both route over the public internet, and Front Door is a global entry point for web applications, not a site-to-site connectivity service.

q: Two VMs host a stateful application whose instance count must stay at exactly two. The team wants protection from a single host or rack failure, and wants to avoid both VMs rebooting during the same planned maintenance, all within one datacenter. Which option fits?
opts: Place both VMs in an availability set
Create a Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
Put both VMs behind an Azure Load Balancer
Deploy the two VMs in two different regions
why: An availability set spreads a fixed group of VMs across fault domains (separate racks, power, and switches) and update domains (separate maintenance windows) inside one datacenter — precisely the two protections asked for, with no change to instance count. A Scale Set is built to add and remove identical instances on demand, which conflicts with a fixed count of two stateful servers. A Load Balancer distributes traffic but has no say over where the VMs are physically placed. Two regions would protect against far more than a rack failure but adds latency and complexity the scenario never asked for.

q: A company keeps seven years of compliance archives that are almost never opened. If an auditor requests one, retrieval within a day is acceptable. Storage cost must be as low as possible. Which blob access tier fits?
opts: Hot
Cool
Cold
Archive
why: Archive has the lowest storage cost of all tiers, and its trade-off — data is offline and must be rehydrated, which can take hours — is acceptable when a day's retrieval window is fine. Cold is the nearest miss: it is also for rarely accessed data, but it stays online with millisecond access and costs more to store than Archive, so it isn't the lowest-cost choice here. Cool is for data accessed occasionally, and Hot is priced for frequent access — both would pay for responsiveness the scenario explicitly doesn't need.

q: A company's backups must survive the loss of an entire Azure region. The budget owner asks whether zone-redundant storage (ZRS) alone meets that requirement, since it already keeps three copies. Which response is accurate?
opts: No — ZRS keeps every copy inside one region; GRS or GZRS adds a copy in the paired region
Yes — the three ZRS copies are placed in zones that Azure spreads across separate regions
Yes — ZRS fails over automatically to the paired region during a regional outage
No — only LRS can be combined with a paired region for cross-region replication
why: ZRS protects against a datacenter (zone) failure by spreading copies across availability zones, but all of those zones belong to the same region, so a regional outage takes every copy with it. Surviving that needs geo-redundancy — GRS or GZRS — which adds asynchronous replication to the paired region. Zones never span regions, ZRS has no cross-region failover to perform, and LRS is the least redundant option, not a prerequisite for geo-replication.

q: A company wants every engineer to get their own isolated Azure environment for testing, with the company's security policies applied automatically without extra configuration per environment. Which combination enables this?
opts: Separate subscriptions per engineer, grouped under a management group with policy assigned at that level
Separate resource groups per engineer within one subscription, with the same policy assigned individually to each resource group
One resource group shared by all engineers with individual RBAC roles
A separate management group per engineer, each containing its own single subscription with no shared parent
why: Subscriptions give real isolation, and a management group above them lets policy apply automatically to every subscription beneath it — configured once, not per environment. Assigning policy to each resource group individually technically works but requires exactly the repeated configuration the scenario wants to avoid, and separate management groups with no shared parent would still mean setting the policy up once per engineer.

q: Which identity feature lets a partner organization's employees sign into your app using their own company credentials, without you creating accounts for them in your directory?
opts: Conditional Access
External identities
Azure RBAC
A dynamic security group
why: External identities let outside users authenticate with their own existing identity rather than a new account in your directory. Conditional Access and RBAC both assume the user already has some identity in your system; a dynamic security group just auto-manages membership for accounts that already exist.

q: A company wants to require MFA only when an employee signs in from a country they've never signed in from before, but not on every sign-in. Which feature enables this specific, condition-based rule?
opts: Conditional Access
External identities
Enabling multifactor authentication for all users
Azure RBAC
why: Conditional Access applies rules based on conditions like sign-in location, layering MFA on only when a condition is met. Enabling MFA for all users would require it on every sign-in regardless of location, which is more than this scenario asks for.

q: A contractor signs in to the Azure portal from a compliant laptop but gets 'access denied' when restarting a VM. From an unmanaged tablet, the sign-in itself is blocked before the portal loads. Which pairing explains the two outcomes?
opts: The restart failure is an Azure RBAC gap; the blocked tablet sign-in is Conditional Access
The restart failure is Conditional Access; the blocked tablet sign-in is an Azure RBAC gap
Both outcomes come from Conditional Access evaluating the device and the action
Both outcomes come from Azure RBAC, since role assignments can be scoped to a device
why: The contractor could sign in from the laptop, so Conditional Access let them through; being unable to restart a VM once inside is a missing permission, which is RBAC's domain. Blocking the sign-in entirely from an unmanaged device is a device-compliance condition — classic Conditional Access, evaluated before any resource is touched. Conditional Access decides whether and how a sign-in happens; it does not grant or deny individual resource actions. RBAC assigns roles to identities at a scope such as a resource group, never to a device.

q: A scenario describes an attacker compromising the network perimeter, but still being unable to access application data without passing separate identity and device checks. Which principle does this describe?
opts: A perimeter-based security model
Zero Trust
Least-privilege access
Network segmentation with NSGs
why: Zero Trust means never assuming trust based on network location — every request is verified on identity, device, and context, so breaching the perimeter alone grants nothing. A perimeter-based model is the opposite assumption: once inside, traffic is trusted, which is exactly what fails here. Least privilege limits how much an already-authenticated identity can do, but it isn't the principle that demands separate identity and device checks on each request. NSG segmentation filters network traffic by IP and port; it does not verify who or what device is making the request.

q: A new administrator is asked to produce, with no setup work, a list of concrete changes to existing resources that would cut cost, improve resilience, and tighten security, based on Azure's own analysis of their configuration. Which tool should they open first?
opts: Azure Monitor
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Advisor
An Azure Well-Architected Review assessment
why: Advisor continuously analyzes your deployed resources and surfaces specific recommendations across cost, reliability, performance, security, and operational excellence — free and with nothing to configure. Defender for Cloud is the near-miss: it also recommends changes, but only for security posture, so it misses the cost and resilience asks. Monitor collects metrics and logs and raises alerts; it doesn't recommend configuration changes. A Well-Architected Review is a questionnaire-based self-assessment of a workload's design, not an automated scan of what is actually deployed.

q: A company needs to move 200 TB of on-premises data into Azure Blob Storage, but their internet connection would take months to transfer it. Which service is designed for this scenario?
opts: Azure File Sync
Azure Migrate
Azure Data Box
AzCopy over a site-to-site VPN
why: Data Box is a physical device for transferring very large datasets offline when network transfer isn't practical. AzCopy over a VPN is still limited by the same slow internet connection — it doesn't solve the bottleneck, just moves it onto an encrypted tunnel.

q: Which tool would an administrator use to script bulk, one-time file copies between an on-premises server and Azure Blob Storage from the command line?
opts: Azure File Sync
AzCopy
Azure Migrate
Azure Storage Explorer
why: AzCopy is the command-line tool built for scripted transfers. Storage Explorer offers similar transfer capability but through a GUI, not a script; File Sync is for ongoing, continuous synchronization rather than a one-time scripted copy; and Migrate is for assessing and moving whole workloads, not files.

q: A company wants to manage on-premises servers and VMs in another cloud using the same Azure tools, like Azure Policy and RBAC, that they already use for native Azure resources. Which service enables this?
opts: Azure Monitor
Azure Migrate
A hybrid Microsoft Entra Connect deployment
Azure Arc
why: Azure Arc extends Azure management tooling — including Policy and RBAC — to resources outside Azure. Migrate assesses and moves workloads rather than managing them afterward, Monitor only collects telemetry, and Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes identities, not resource governance.

q: A company deploys VMs across two availability zones in the same region for resilience. Which failure scenario would this NOT protect against?
opts: A single rack failing within one zone
A single datacenter losing power
A cooling failure in one zone's datacenter
The entire Azure region becoming unavailable
why: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level failures within a region — power, cooling, or a single rack going down in one zone — because the other zone keeps running. They don't protect against a failure of the region itself, which needs geo-redundancy or a multi-region design.

q: An application needs to authenticate a service, not a person, to access Azure resources without embedding a password in code. Which Entra ID feature fits?
opts: A guest user account created for the application
Self-service password reset applied to a service account
A dynamic security group containing the application
A managed identity
why: A managed identity lets an Azure resource authenticate to other services automatically, with Azure handling the credential entirely — nothing is embedded in code. The other three all still rely on a password or an account meant for a human, which is exactly what this scenario is trying to avoid.

q: If the region chosen for a resource group suffers an outage, the resources in that group that were deployed to other regions stop running as well.
opts: True
False
why: A resource group's region only determines where the group's metadata is stored. The resources inside can live in any region, and they keep running on their own regional infrastructure regardless of what happens to the metadata region — at most, management operations on the group could be affected while it is unreachable. The statement treats the group as a runtime boundary when it is only a logical management container.

q: Deleting a resource group removes every resource it contains, and deleting a management group likewise removes the subscriptions beneath it.
opts: True
False
why: The first half is true and the second half is the trap. A resource group owns the lifecycle of its resources, so deleting it deletes everything inside. A management group is only an organizational container for subscriptions: it must be empty before it can be deleted, and moving subscriptions out of it (back to the tenant root group or elsewhere) leaves them intact. The exam likes to test that the two containers behave differently on deletion.

q: Placing two virtual machines in the same availability set guarantees that they run in different availability zones.
opts: True
False
why: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains and update domains — separate racks and separate maintenance windows — within a single datacenter. It says nothing about zones; both VMs can be, and normally are, in the same zone. Protection from a whole datacenter failing requires explicitly deploying the VMs into different availability zones, which is a separate choice (and the two options are mutually exclusive for a given VM). Confusing the two is one of the most common AZ-900 errors.

q: A company that must encrypt its ExpressRoute traffic in transit has to configure that encryption itself — for example with IPsec or MACsec — because the circuit does not encrypt traffic by default.
opts: True
False
why: ExpressRoute's security comes from being a private, dedicated path that never touches the public internet, not from encryption. If a compliance rule requires encryption in transit, the customer adds it — a site-to-site VPN over the ExpressRoute private peering, or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct. The contrast is VPN Gateway, which is encrypted (IPsec) precisely because it crosses the internet. Assuming 'private' means 'encrypted' is the mistake this statement is written to catch.

q: An application using a storage account configured with geo-redundant storage (GRS) can read from the secondary region at any time, even before a failover is initiated.
opts: True
False
why: Plain GRS replicates data to the paired region, but that secondary copy is not accessible until a failover makes it the new primary. Read access to the secondary at any time is exactly what the read-access variants — RA-GRS and RA-GZRS — add, and that distinction is what you are paying for when you choose them. An app designed to serve reads from the secondary during a primary outage needs RA-GRS; with GRS it would simply fail until failover.

q: Assigning an Azure Policy with a Deny effect automatically deletes existing resources that already violate the rule.
opts: True
False
why: Deny blocks new or updated deployments that would violate the rule. Resources that already exist are evaluated and reported as non-compliant on the policy's compliance dashboard, but Policy never deletes them. Bringing them into line is a separate remediation step — manual changes, or a remediation task for policies with DeployIfNotExists or Modify effects. The statement credits Policy with a destructive power it does not have, which is a frequent misconception.

q: Adding a private endpoint to an Azure SQL Database automatically disables the database's public endpoint.
opts: True
False
why: A private endpoint adds a private IP for the service inside your VNet, so traffic from that network stays on the Microsoft backbone — but it is an addition, not a replacement. The public endpoint remains reachable until you separately turn off public network access (or restrict it with firewall rules). Teams that stop after creating the private endpoint have not actually reduced internet exposure, which is the gap this statement tests.

q: A Conditional Access policy can require multifactor authentication from a user who holds no Azure RBAC role in any subscription.
opts: True
False
why: Conditional Access operates in Microsoft Entra ID at sign-in time and can be scoped to any user, group, or application — it has no dependency on Azure RBAC, which only governs what an identity can do with Azure resources after signing in. A user with zero Azure role assignments can still be required to pass MFA to reach Microsoft 365 or any other cloud app. Treating the two as linked, or assuming Conditional Access only matters for Azure administrators, is the misconception here.

q: Which two resources are required to establish a site-to-site VPN connection between an on-premises network and Azure? (Choose two.)
opts: Local Network Gateway
VPN Gateway
ExpressRoute
Azure Bastion
why: A site-to-site VPN needs a VPN Gateway on the Azure side and a Local Network Gateway representing the on-premises side. ExpressRoute is a separate, non-VPN connection type, and Bastion is unrelated to site-to-site connectivity.

q: All four of these are real Azure Storage redundancy options. Which two replicate data to a second, geographically separate region? (Choose two.)
opts: Locally-redundant storage (LRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
why: GRS and GZRS both add asynchronous replication to a secondary, paired region on top of their base redundancy. LRS keeps all copies in one datacenter, and ZRS spreads copies across zones within the same region — neither one leaves that region.

q: A company is choosing between an availability set and availability zones for a two-VM application that must stay in one region. Which two statements should guide the decision? (Choose two.)
opts: Zones protect against an entire datacenter failing; an availability set does not
An availability set spreads VMs across racks and maintenance windows inside one datacenter
Zones automatically replicate the VMs to the region's paired region
VMs must be placed in an availability set before they can be assigned to zones
why: The hinge between the two features is the failure they protect against. An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (racks) and update domains (maintenance windows) within a single datacenter, so it survives a rack or host failure. Availability zones put VMs in physically separate datacenters within the region, so they also survive one datacenter losing power or cooling. Zones never replicate anything to another region — that is a different design — and the two features are alternatives for a given VM, not a prerequisite chain.

q: A team has two workloads: a legacy Windows application that needs a custom kernel driver, and a two-minute cleanup job that runs each night. Which two pairings match each workload to the most fitting compute service? (Choose two.)
opts: Azure Virtual Machines for the legacy application
Azure Functions for the nightly cleanup job
Azure App Service for the legacy application
Azure Container Instances for the legacy application
why: A custom kernel driver requires control of the operating system itself, which only a virtual machine (IaaS) provides. A short, scheduled job that runs for two minutes a day is the textbook serverless case: a timer-triggered Function bills only for those minutes and needs no server left running. App Service and Container Instances are the near-misses for the legacy app — both can host Windows workloads — but neither lets you install kernel-level drivers into a managed platform's OS, so they fail the stated requirement.

q: An administrator plans several changes to the company's Azure hierarchy. Which two of the planned actions are actually possible? (Choose two.)
opts: Assign the Reader role at a management group so it is inherited by every subscription beneath it
Move a subscription out of one management group and into another
Place a single resource group under two subscriptions so both can bill for it
Nest a management group underneath a subscription to subdivide it
why: Role assignments and policies made at a management group flow down to all subscriptions, resource groups, and resources beneath it, and subscriptions can be moved between management groups as an organization changes. The hierarchy is strict in the other direction: a resource group belongs to exactly one subscription, and management groups sit only above subscriptions — you subdivide a subscription with resource groups, never with another management group.

q: One developer needs to run a single container for a 20-minute batch job with no orchestration. Another team needs a set of HTTP microservices that scale to zero when idle, without managing a cluster. Which two pairings fit? (Choose two.)
opts: Azure Container Instances for the 20-minute batch job
Azure Container Apps for the scale-to-zero microservices
Azure Kubernetes Service for the 20-minute batch job
Azure Container Instances for the scale-to-zero microservices
why: Container Instances is the fastest way to run one container on demand and let it finish, with nothing to orchestrate — ideal for a short batch job. Container Apps is built for microservices: it hides the Kubernetes cluster, handles HTTP ingress, and scales each service down to zero replicas when idle. AKS could run the batch job but would mean standing up and paying for a whole cluster for one container. Container Instances can't satisfy the microservices need because it has no built-in autoscaling or scale-to-zero — each instance runs until stopped.

q: A company has an ExpressRoute circuit to Azure and is reviewing its resiliency and security design. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: A site-to-site VPN Gateway can serve as a failover path if the ExpressRoute circuit goes down
Traffic on the circuit is not encrypted unless the company adds its own encryption
When the private circuit is congested, ExpressRoute traffic is automatically rerouted over the public internet
Having ExpressRoute removes the need for network security groups on the Azure virtual network
why: ExpressRoute and a VPN Gateway can coexist, and a common design uses the VPN as a cheaper backup path for the dedicated circuit. ExpressRoute's isolation comes from being private, not from encryption, so sensitive traffic still needs IPsec or MACsec layered on. The circuit never falls back to the internet — that would defeat its purpose; congestion is handled by bandwidth choice and redundant circuits. And a private connection says nothing about what traffic is allowed between subnets, so NSGs are still the traffic-filtering control inside the VNet.

q: A company's backup data must survive a regional outage, and its recovery application must be able to read that data from the secondary region during the outage without waiting for a failover. Which two statements are accurate for choosing a redundancy option? (Choose two.)
opts: RA-GRS (or RA-GZRS) allows the application to read from the secondary region at any time
Plain GRS replicates to the paired region but the secondary cannot be read until a failover
ZRS satisfies the regional-outage requirement at a lower cost than GRS
LRS is sufficient because its three copies are kept on separate racks
why: The requirement has two parts — survive a region loss, and read from the secondary before failover — and only the read-access geo options satisfy both. GRS gets the data to the paired region but keeps the secondary unreadable until failover, so it fails the second requirement. ZRS keeps every copy inside one region, so it fails the first, no matter how much cheaper it is. LRS's three copies on separate racks protect against hardware failure in one datacenter and nothing wider.

q: A security team wants to block the finance app for sign-ins from non-compliant devices, and separately wants to give the finance team Contributor rights on their resource group. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Conditional Access can block access to the finance app when the device is not marked compliant
Conditional Access cannot grant Contributor; that requires an Azure RBAC role assignment
Conditional Access evaluates only external guest users, so employees would be unaffected
Assigning the Contributor role can itself enforce multifactor authentication at sign-in
why: Device compliance is one of the signals Conditional Access evaluates, and blocking a specific cloud app on that basis is a standard policy. Granting permissions on Azure resources is a different job entirely — only an RBAC role assignment at the resource-group scope gives Contributor rights. Conditional Access applies to any identity you scope it to, employees included, and an RBAC role carries no authentication requirements of its own; MFA is enforced by Conditional Access, not by the role.

q: A company wants to allow inbound traffic only on port 443 to a subnet of web servers and block all other inbound ports, without deploying a separate firewall appliance. Which Azure feature fits?
opts: VNet peering to a separate management subnet that already has the desired port rules
A network security group (NSG) with allow/deny rules on the subnet
A Read-only resource lock applied to the subnet to prevent configuration changes
Azure Policy with a Deny effect blocking noncompliant inbound rules
why: A network security group filters inbound and outbound traffic by port, protocol, and IP at the subnet or NIC level — exactly this scenario. A resource lock only blocks delete/modify of the resource's own configuration, not live network packets; Azure Policy governs configuration compliance, not traffic filtering; and peering just connects two VNets without adding any port-level filtering of its own.

q: A web app in one region needs incoming HTTPS requests sent to different backend pools by URL path (/images versus /api) and protected by a web application firewall. The entry point must sit inside the company's VNet with a private frontend IP. Which service fits?
opts: Azure Front Door
Azure Traffic Manager
Azure Load Balancer
Azure Application Gateway
why: Application Gateway is a regional Layer-7 load balancer: it routes by URL path or host header, offers an integrated WAF, and is deployed into a subnet of your VNet, so it can expose a private frontend. Front Door is the near-miss — it also does path routing and WAF — but it is a global edge service with a public frontend that cannot be placed inside a VNet. Traffic Manager is DNS-based and steers clients to endpoints without inspecting HTTP at all. Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and has no concept of URL paths or a WAF.

q: A platform team runs dozens of containerized microservices. It needs direct access to the Kubernetes API to install custom operators and a service mesh, and wants control over node pool sizes and the node operating system. Which service fits?
opts: Azure Container Apps
Azure Container Instances
Azure App Service for Containers
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
why: AKS is managed Kubernetes: Azure runs the control plane, but you still get the full Kubernetes API, choose node pool sizes and images, and can install operators or a mesh of your choice. Container Apps is the near-miss — it also runs microservices with scaling and is built on Kubernetes underneath — but it deliberately hides the cluster, so there is no Kubernetes API or node pool to manage. Container Instances runs individual containers with no orchestration at all, and App Service for Containers hosts a web app's container inside the App Service platform, not a cluster you control.

q: An organization wants to stop running its own name servers and instead have Microsoft's global network answer public queries for contoso.com, including its MX records for mail. Which service should they use?
opts: Azure Private DNS zones
Azure Traffic Manager
Azure Front Door
Azure DNS
why: Azure DNS hosts public DNS zones — A, CNAME, MX, and the rest — on Microsoft's global anycast name servers, which is exactly 'answer public queries for our domain.' Private DNS zones are the near-miss: same record types, but they resolve only inside linked virtual networks and are invisible to the internet, so public mail routing would break. Traffic Manager is DNS-based, but it steers clients among endpoints you register; it isn't an authoritative host for a whole domain and can't serve MX records. Front Door is an application delivery and routing layer, not a DNS zone host.

q: Which two statements about Bicep are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Bicep can only define compute resources, not networking or storage
Bicep deployments run through the same underlying Azure Resource Manager as ARM templates
Bicep is a simpler, more concise language that compiles down to ARM template JSON
Bicep replaces the need for Azure CLI and PowerShell entirely
why: Bicep is a domain-specific language that transpiles to standard ARM JSON and deploys through the same Resource Manager engine as ARM templates — it's a friendlier authoring format, not a different deployment mechanism. It can define any Azure resource type, not just compute, and CLI/PowerShell are still used to trigger a Bicep deployment, not replaced by it.

q: An application needs a NoSQL database that stays available with low-latency reads and writes across users on three different continents, automatically replicating data close to each region. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
opts: Azure Table storage
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure SQL Database
Azure Queue storage
why: Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database designed specifically for low-latency access across multiple regions, with data automatically replicated to wherever it is configured. Azure SQL Database is a relational, not NoSQL, PaaS database, and while it supports some geo-replication, it is not the multi-region, low-latency-by-design NoSQL service this scenario calls for. Table storage is a simpler NoSQL key-value store without Cosmos DB's global distribution features, and Queue storage is for messaging, not for serving application data reads at all.

q: A development team wants to add image recognition to their app that can identify objects in a photo, without collecting training data or building and training their own model. Which Azure service fits best?
opts: Azure Machine Learning
Azure Databricks
Foundry Tools (formerly Azure AI services)
Azure Synapse Analytics
why: Foundry Tools (formerly Azure AI services, and before that Cognitive Services) provide pre-built, ready-to-call AI models, including image recognition, so a team can add this capability without training anything themselves. Azure Machine Learning is the opposite fit here — it is the platform for building, training, and deploying a custom model. Azure Databricks and Azure Synapse Analytics are both big-data analytics and processing platforms, not prebuilt AI capabilities.

q: A manufacturer needs to securely connect and manage two million factory sensors, with reliable two-way communication between each device and the cloud. Which Azure service is designed for this?
opts: Azure Logic Apps
Azure Event Grid
Azure Service Bus
Azure IoT Hub
why: IoT Hub is purpose-built as a central message hub for secure, bi-directional communication between IoT devices and the cloud, and is designed to scale to large device fleets like this. Event Grid and Service Bus are both general-purpose messaging services, not designed specifically for device identity, provisioning, and device-to-cloud or cloud-to-device patterns at IoT scale, and Logic Apps is a workflow automation tool, not a device connectivity service.

q: A team wants databases where Microsoft patches the engine and operating system. It needs a relational T-SQL database for its ERP and a globally distributed NoSQL store for a mobile app. Which two choices meet both the management and the workload requirements? (Choose two.)
opts: Azure SQL Database for the relational ERP workload
Azure Cosmos DB for the globally distributed NoSQL workload
SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine for the relational ERP workload
Azure Table Storage for the globally distributed NoSQL workload
why: Azure SQL Database is fully managed relational T-SQL, and Cosmos DB is the managed NoSQL service designed for multi-region replication with low latency — both are PaaS, so Microsoft handles engine and OS patching. SQL Server on a VM meets the T-SQL need but fails the management requirement, because the team would patch the OS and engine itself. Table Storage is managed NoSQL, but it is a simple key-value store without Cosmos DB's turnkey global distribution, so it misses the workload requirement.

q: A company deploys one VM in each of the three availability zones of East US. A manager concludes the app is now protected from an East US-wide outage because 'each zone is effectively its own region.' Which correction is accurate?
opts: Zones are separate datacenters inside East US; surviving a regional outage needs a second region
The manager is right: Azure treats each zone as an independent region for failover purposes
Zones protect against regional outages only once GRS storage is attached to the VMs
Three zones automatically replicate the VMs to the East US paired region
why: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within one region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking. They protect against a datacenter failing, but an event that takes out the whole region takes every zone in it. Regional protection requires deploying to a second region (typically the paired region) and failing over to it. Zones are never treated as regions; GRS protects storage data, not running VMs; and nothing about using zones replicates VMs anywhere else.

q: A company organizes its Azure resources so that a single resource group contains both a production web app in East US and its paired database in West US, deployed together for a coordinated app release. Is this a valid resource group design?
opts: No, because a resource group can only contain resources from a single Azure region
Yes, because a resource group is a management boundary, not a regional one
No, because paired regions must be managed in strictly separate resource groups for compliance reasons
Yes, but only if both resources are deployed using the same ARM template
why: A resource group is a logical container for managing related resources together (it is a management boundary, not a billing boundary) — it can hold resources from multiple regions, as this scenario does. It isn't restricted to one region, there's no rule requiring paired-region resources to sit in separate groups, and using a shared ARM template isn't a precondition for this being valid.

q: A hospital network would ideally link its on-premises datacenter to Azure over a private circuit, but its budget and timeline can't absorb the weeks-long provisioning a dedicated connection usually requires. It needs an encrypted network-to-network link running within days. Which option best fits both constraints?
opts: ExpressRoute, since it provides the most complete isolation from the public internet of any connectivity option
A site-to-site VPN Gateway, since it can be provisioned quickly and still encrypts traffic over the internet
Azure Bastion, since it provides secure remote access with very little provisioning delay
Azure Front Door, since it routes traffic through Microsoft's global network instead of the public internet
why: A VPN Gateway can be stood up in hours over the existing internet connection, trading ExpressRoute's stronger internet isolation for something that actually fits this budget and timeline — the imaging workload still gets an encrypted, private-feeling tunnel. ExpressRoute is the hospital's ideal on isolation and latency, but its multi-week circuit provisioning is exactly what the scenario rules out. Bastion is for secure administrative access to VMs, not site-to-site connectivity between networks, and Front Door is a web-application entry point, not a private network connection.

q: An architect documents geo-redundant storage for a Brazil South deployment and writes that Brazil South and its paired region back each other up within the same geography. Which correction is accurate?
opts: Brazil South is paired in both directions with another region inside the Brazil geography, so the statement is correct
Brazil South has no pair at all, so geo-redundant storage is not available for deployments there
Brazil South is paired one way with South Central US, which is outside the Brazil geography, and South Central US is not paired back
Brazil South is paired in both directions with East US, which is outside its geography
why: Brazil South is the documented exception: it is paired in only one direction with South Central US, a region outside its own geography, while South Central US is not paired back to Brazil South. Most pairs are bidirectional and within one geography, which is what makes this a trap. The claim that it has no pair is wrong because the pairing exists, and pairing with East US has no basis.

q: A team deploys to Poland Central, which has no traditional region pair. Their compliance lead asks how resiliency is typically provided there. Which answer matches Microsoft's description?
opts: The region relies on availability zones and geo-redundant storage instead of a traditional pair
Such regions have no resiliency options available beyond a single datacenter
Customers must move to a sovereign region such as Azure Government to get redundancy
Microsoft automatically fails workloads over to the nearest paired region
why: Regions without a traditional pair, including Italy North, Poland Central, and Israel Central, rely on availability zones and geo-redundant storage for resiliency. No pair also means no automatic failover to a partner region, and it does not mean resiliency is unavailable. Sovereign regions are a separate compliance concept and are not a way to add redundancy.

q: A Chinese subsidiary must run on Azure regions that are physically and logically isolated from global Azure, in a model where Microsoft does not directly maintain the datacenters but works through a partner. Which option matches?
opts: Azure Government regions, operated for U.S. agencies by screened U.S. personnel
An Azure availability zone inside a global Azure region
A region pair within the Asia Pacific geography, run by Microsoft directly
Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (China East, China North)
why: The China regions are available through a partnership between Microsoft and 21Vianet, so Microsoft does not directly maintain those datacenters, and they are a sovereign region. Azure Government is the near miss: it is also isolated but serves U.S. government agencies and partners and is operated by screened U.S. personnel. A region pair is a resiliency relationship and an availability zone is a location inside a region, so neither is an isolated cloud instance.

q: Which of these Azure resources is described as zonal, meaning you pin it to a specific availability zone, rather than replicated across zones for you?
opts: A zone-redundant storage account
A virtual machine
Azure DNS
Microsoft Entra ID
why: VMs, managed disks, and IP addresses are zonal services: you choose the zone and any spreading across zones is your design. Zone-redundant storage is the opposite pattern, where the platform replicates across zones automatically. Azure DNS and Microsoft Entra ID are non-regional services that are always available from Azure geographies and resilient to zone-wide outages.

q: A batch of CPU-intensive application tiers needs the best fit among VM families, while a separate dev/test box only needs occasional CPU spikes at low cost. Which pair of families matches these two needs?
opts: N-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and M-series for the dev/test box
E-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and F-series for the dev/test box
B-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and E-series for the dev/test box
F-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and B-series for the dev/test box
why: F-series is compute optimized, which suits CPU-intensive tiers, and B-series is burstable and cost-efficient, which suits dev/test workloads with occasional spikes. E-series is memory optimized, M-series is for very large memory footprints, and N-series is GPU-enabled, so the other pairings each assign a family to a job it is not built for.

q: An administrator sees the VM size name D2s_v5 in a deployment template. Which reading of that name is correct?
opts: D means disk optimized, 2 is the amount of RAM in GB, s means standard HDD, and v5 is the vCPU count
D means database workloads only, 2 is the number of data disks, s means spot pricing, and v5 is the Windows version
D means general purpose, 2 is the number of vCPUs, s indicates Premium SSD support, and v5 is the hardware generation
D is the datacenter, 2 is the zone, s is the subscription type, and v5 is the API version
why: In VM naming, the letter is the family (D is general purpose), the number is the vCPU count, a lowercase s indicates Premium SSD support, and the version is the hardware generation. The other readings invent meanings: D is not disk, the number is not RAM or data disks, s is not HDD or spot pricing, and nothing in the name encodes datacenter or zone.

q: A technician deletes a virtual machine from the Azure portal, yet the subscription's monthly cost drops by much less than expected. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: Deleting a VM only pauses billing for the VM for one month before charges resume
Azure Policy adds a small charge for each deleted resource in a subscription
Reservations always keep billing the full VM price after a VM is deleted, whatever its size
The VM's disks, network interface, or public IP address were not deleted with it and still incur charges
why: Provisioning a VM creates companion resources such as storage disks, a network interface, and often a public IP address, and removing the VM does not always remove them. Those leftovers can keep billing until they are cleaned up. Billing does not merely pause for a month, a reservation is a pricing commitment that is unrelated to deletion, and Azure Policy has no per-deletion charge.

q: A support center runs three rotating shifts. Management wants every agent to get the same centrally managed Windows desktop, reachable from personal laptops and tablets, with data kept in Azure rather than on the devices. Which service fits best?
opts: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure App Service
Azure Bastion
why: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops and apps hosted in Azure to many device types, integrates with Microsoft Entra ID, and keeps data in Azure-hosted sessions. Scale Sets are groups of identical VMs for scaling applications, not a desktop delivery service. Bastion gives administrators secure RDP and SSH access to VMs, and App Service hosts web apps and APIs.

q: A web application must run a script every night in the same context as the app, and the team wants to avoid managing any extra servers. Which App Service capability fits?
opts: A private endpoint
An availability set
A VPN Gateway
WebJobs
why: WebJobs run a program or script in the same context as a web, API, or mobile app, either on a schedule or on a trigger, and are commonly used for background tasks. An availability set groups VMs for resiliency, a VPN Gateway is a network connectivity service, and a private endpoint is a networking feature, so none of them runs scheduled code.

q: A security team wants Azure SQL Database to be reachable through a private IP address taken from their own virtual network's address space. Which feature provides that?
opts: A service endpoint
Virtual network peering
A private endpoint
A public IP address on the database server
why: A private endpoint exists inside your virtual network and uses a private IP address from that network's address space, so the service is reached privately. A service endpoint is the near miss: it gives an optimized route on the Azure backbone and lets you restrict the service to chosen subnets, but it does not give the service a private IP in your address space. Peering connects two virtual networks, and a public IP is the opposite of what was asked.

q: A consultant working from hotels needs an encrypted connection from a laptop into an Azure virtual network, and there is no VPN hardware at any of the hotels. Which connection type fits?
opts: Point-to-site VPN
Site-to-site VPN
ExpressRoute
Virtual network peering
why: A point-to-site connection lets an individual client computer start an encrypted VPN connection into the virtual network, with no on-premises VPN device needed. Site-to-site links an on-premises VPN device or gateway to Azure, so it fits an office rather than a laptop. ExpressRoute needs a connectivity provider and a private circuit, and peering connects two virtual networks to each other.

q: A company has ExpressRoute and states that none of its traffic to Microsoft ever crosses the public internet. Which fact shows that this claim is too strong?
opts: ExpressRoute encrypts every packet with IPsec by default, so internet exposure is impossible
ExpressRoute connects only to Microsoft 365 and never reaches Azure compute or storage services
DNS queries, certificate revocation list checks, and Azure Content Delivery Network requests are still sent over the public internet
ExpressRoute traffic is always routed through the VPN Gateway before reaching Microsoft
why: Even with ExpressRoute, DNS queries, certificate revocation list checks, and Azure CDN requests still use the public internet, so the claim overstates the isolation. ExpressRoute is a private connection and is not encrypted by default, so saying it encrypts everything is wrong. It connects to Azure services and also to Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365, and it is not routed through VPN Gateway.

q: A trading application stores many small objects in Blob Storage and needs very high transaction rates with consistently low latency. Which storage account type does Microsoft recommend for this?
opts: Standard general-purpose v2
Premium block blobs
Premium file shares
Premium page blobs
why: Premium block blobs are the premium type for block and append blobs, recommended for high transaction rates, smaller objects, and consistently low storage latency. Standard general-purpose v2 is the broad default but not the low-latency tier. Premium page blobs are for page blobs only, and premium file shares are for Azure Files rather than blob objects.

q: Records must be kept at least 90 days, are rarely read, and must stay immediately readable with no rehydration wait. Which access tier gives the lowest storage cost that still meets these needs?
opts: Hot
Cool
Archive
Cold
why: Cold is optimized for data that is rarely accessed, stored at least 90 days, and still needs fast retrieval; it costs less to store than Cool and more to access. Archive is cheapest but is offline and needs rehydration, which breaks the immediate-read requirement. Cool is aimed at data kept at least 30 days and costs more to store than Cold, and Hot is the most expensive to store.

q: A company uses geo-redundant storage. The primary region is lost before the most recent writes finished replicating. What does the replication design predict?
opts: Nothing is lost because GRS copies every write synchronously to the secondary region
Recent writes not yet copied to the secondary can be lost, and the gap is described by the recovery point objective
All data is lost because GRS keeps only a single copy of each object in one place
Only reads fail, because writes are always fully replicated before they are acknowledged
why: GRS copies data synchronously three times in the primary region and then asynchronously to the secondary, so a failure can lose writes not yet replicated. The window is the recovery point objective, typically under 15 minutes although there is no SLA on replication time. Synchronous replication to the secondary is not how GRS works, a single copy is never kept, and writes are not guaranteed to be replicated before the failure.

q: A branch office wants its local Windows file server to keep working as a cache: frequently used files stay on local disk, rarely used files live in Azure, and changes flow in both directions. Which solution fits?
opts: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering
AzCopy sync run on a nightly schedule
Azure Data Box shipped to the branch office
Azure Storage Explorer installed on the server
