why: Azure File Sync keeps a Windows server bidirectionally synchronized with an Azure Files share, and cloud tiering keeps hot files local while rarely used files stay in the cloud until requested. AzCopy sync only copies in one direction between a source and destination you designate. Data Box is a one-time shipped device, and Storage Explorer is a GUI for managing storage rather than a continuous sync service.

q: A company lifts a legacy application onto Azure VMs. It depends on LDAP binds, Kerberos or NTLM authentication, and Group Policy, and the team does not want to deploy or patch domain controllers. Users already exist in Microsoft Entra ID. What fits best?
opts: Microsoft Entra Connect installed on the VMs
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Azure RBAC with custom roles
A Conditional Access policy for the application
why: Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain with domain join, group policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM without you running domain controllers, and users sign in with their existing credentials. Entra Connect synchronizes an on-premises Active Directory with Entra ID, so it does not provide those domain services. RBAC controls what identities can do with Azure resources, and Conditional Access governs the conditions of sign-in.

q: Which statement correctly describes how Microsoft Entra Domain Services receives identity information?
opts: It synchronizes in both directions with Microsoft Entra ID, so objects created in the managed domain appear in Entra ID
It stores no user accounts, so every user and group has to be recreated by hand in the managed domain
It reads identities only from an on-premises Active Directory and never from Microsoft Entra ID at all
It performs one-way synchronization from Microsoft Entra ID into the managed domain, and resources created directly in the managed domain are not synchronized back
why: A managed domain is configured for one-way synchronization from Microsoft Entra ID, and objects created directly in the managed domain do not flow back to Entra ID. In a hybrid setup, Entra Connect brings on-premises identities into Entra ID first, which then syncs to the managed domain. Two-way sync and manual recreation are both inaccurate, and it is not limited to on-premises Active Directory.

q: Executives want to sign in by tapping a hardware key plugged into a USB port, with no password typed and strong resistance to phishing. Which passwordless method does this describe?
opts: Windows Hello for Business
FIDO2 security key
Microsoft Authenticator number matching
A password plus an SMS code
why: FIDO2 security keys are hardware devices, typically USB but also Bluetooth or NFC, that handle authentication without a username or password and are phishing-resistant. Windows Hello for Business ties credentials to a user's own Windows PC, and the Authenticator app uses a phone notification with number matching. A password plus an SMS code is multifactor authentication, not passwordless, because the password is still used.

q: A project team invites supplier employees to a SharePoint site. The suppliers sign in with their own work credentials and show up in the company's directory as guest users. Which Microsoft Entra External ID capability is this?
opts: B2B collaboration
B2B direct connect
Microsoft Entra External ID for customers
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
why: B2B collaboration lets external users sign in with their preferred identity to your applications and represents them in your directory, typically as guest users. B2B direct connect is a mutual trust with another tenant that currently supports Teams shared channels, and those users are not represented in your directory. External ID for customers targets consumer-facing apps, and Domain Services is a managed domain service unrelated to guests.

q: Guests from a finished project still have access to several resources. Security wants guest owners or managers to periodically confirm who still needs access, with access removed for those who do not. Which feature fits?
opts: Resource locks
Azure Policy deny effect
Access reviews
Azure Advisor
why: Access reviews ask guests or a decision maker to recertify continued access, and access can then be removed for people who no longer need it. Resource locks only prevent deleting or changing resources, Policy governs resource configuration rather than people, and Advisor offers configuration recommendations.

q: An Owner role is assigned to a user at a management group that contains three subscriptions. A colleague says the role applies only to the management group object itself. What is accurate?
opts: The role is inherited, so the user can manage everything in all three subscriptions beneath the management group
The role applies only if the same assignment is repeated separately on each subscription
The role applies only to resources that are created after the assignment was made
The role is inherited by the subscriptions but not by the resource groups beneath them
why: Azure RBAC is hierarchical: access granted at a parent scope is inherited by all child scopes, so Owner at a management group covers every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath it. No repetition is needed, timing of resource creation does not matter, and inheritance continues all the way down rather than stopping at subscriptions.

q: Which Defender for Cloud capability reduces exposure to brute-force attacks against VM management ports by keeping those ports closed until access is requested?
opts: Azure Policy tag inheritance
A Delete resource lock
The Azure Advisor performance score
Just-in-time VM access
why: Just-in-time VM access is one of the network protections Defender for Cloud offers to reduce brute-force exposure, opening management ports only when needed. A Delete lock stops resource deletion, an Advisor score is a recommendation metric, and tag inheritance is a cost-organization behavior; none of them controls port exposure.

q: A storage account name may include uppercase letters and hyphens, as long as it is unique within its resource group.
opts: True
False
why: Storage account names must be 3 to 24 characters long, using lowercase letters and numbers only, and must be unique across all of Azure because the name forms the account's endpoint. Uppercase letters and hyphens are not allowed, and uniqueness within a resource group is not enough.

q: Azure Data Box can only be used to import data into Azure; it cannot be used to export data out of Azure.
opts: True
False
why: A Data Box order can be an import or an export. Exporting large datasets from Azure for recovery or regulatory needs is a listed scenario, along with one-time bulk migration and periodic large uploads where online transfer is too slow.

q: If one role assignment gives a user Reader on a resource group and another gives the same user Contributor on that group, the user ends up with only the more restrictive permissions.
opts: True
False
why: Azure RBAC uses an allow model, so assignments add up. The user has both the read permissions and the additional write permissions, which means Contributor-level access on that group. Restricting access takes a different mechanism, not a second, narrower role assignment.

q: Which two statements about Azure VPN Gateway are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It is deployed in a dedicated subnet of the virtual network
A virtual network can have only one VPN gateway
A default deployment runs as a single instance with no standby
Traffic between sites travels unencrypted across the internet unless you add a separate encryption layer
why: A VPN gateway is deployed in a dedicated subnet and only one can exist in each virtual network, although that one gateway can connect to multiple locations. By default it runs as two instances in an active/standby configuration, so a single instance is wrong. All data is encrypted inside a private tunnel as it crosses the internet.

q: Which two statements about blob access tiers and scope are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Hot, Cool, and Cold can be set as the account default tier
The Archive tier can be set per blob but not as the account default
Archive can be set as the account default tier
Cool and Cold cost more to store than Hot
why: Hot, Cool, and Cold can be set at the account level, while Archive is only available at the blob level. Cool and Cold have lower storage cost than Hot, with higher access costs, so claiming they cost more to store is backward.

q: Which three of the following are passwordless sign-in options supported by Microsoft Entra ID? (Choose three.)
opts: Windows Hello for Business
Microsoft Authenticator sign-in with number matching and a biometric or PIN
FIDO2 security keys
A password followed by an SMS one-time code
why: Windows Hello for Business, the Authenticator app, and FIDO2 security keys are the three passwordless options. A password followed by an SMS code is multifactor authentication, because the password is still part of the sign-in.

q: Which two statements about Microsoft Defender for Cloud are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It groups recommendations into security controls and calculates a secure score
Its recommendations align with the Microsoft cloud security benchmark
It replaces Azure Policy, which is no longer used underneath it
It can assess only resources that run inside Azure
why: Defender for Cloud groups recommendations into security controls, calculates a secure score, and aligns recommendations to the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. It builds on Azure Policy rather than replacing it, and it also covers on-premises resources through Azure Arc and other clouds such as AWS and GCP.

q: A company wants to prevent a storage account holding compliance data from ever being deleted, even by an administrator who has full Owner permissions on the subscription. Which feature should they apply?
opts: A Delete resource lock
An Azure Policy with an Audit effect
Removing the Owner role from all administrators
A Read-only lock, since it is a stricter version of Delete
why: A resource lock overrides normal RBAC permissions to prevent deletion, regardless of what a user's role otherwise allows — a Delete lock is exactly targeted at this requirement. Removing Owner roles is impractical and self-defeating; an Audit-effect policy only reports non-compliance without blocking anything; and a Read-only lock is stricter in a different way (it also blocks modification) but isn't 'more Delete' than a Delete lock.

q: A company wants to both enforce a rule, like 'no VMs outside East US,' and separately get recommendations for improving cost efficiency of existing resources. Which combination is correct?
opts: Azure Policy for both, since it can also generate cost recommendations
Azure Monitor for enforcement, Azure Policy for recommendations
Azure Advisor for both, since it can also enforce configuration rules
Azure Policy for enforcement, Azure Advisor for recommendations
why: Policy enforces configuration rules going forward; Advisor analyzes existing resources and recommends improvements. Policy doesn't generate recommendations, and Advisor doesn't block or enforce anything — each tool does only one half of this scenario.

q: A company needs to discover and classify sensitive data, like customer SSNs, scattered across multiple data stores in a hybrid environment. Which service is purpose-built for this?
opts: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Policy, using a policy that audits storage account configurations
Azure Advisor, under its security recommendations
Microsoft Purview
why: Purview is specifically for discovering, classifying, and protecting sensitive data, including across hybrid sources. Policy and Advisor both operate on resource configuration, not the content stored inside resources, and Defender for Cloud focuses on threat protection and security posture rather than data classification.

q: An administrator wants to run Azure management commands from a browser on a locked-down machine where they cannot install software. Which tool fits?
opts: The Azure mobile app
Azure Cloud Shell
Azure PowerShell
Azure CLI
why: Cloud Shell runs entirely in the browser with nothing to install, unlike CLI or PowerShell, which are installed locally (though both are also available for use from within Cloud Shell). The Azure mobile app supports monitoring and basic actions, but not the same scripting/command experience.

q: A team deploys environments with a long Azure CLI script that creates resources one by one. Re-running it after a partial failure errors out because some resources already exist. They want deployments that can be safely re-run and whose intended end state lives in source control. What should they adopt?
opts: Declarative templates such as ARM or Bicep
A Read-only lock applied after each successful run
A longer CLI script with delete steps before each create
Azure Advisor operational-excellence recommendations
why: ARM and Bicep templates are declarative: they describe the desired end state, and Resource Manager works out what to create, update, or leave alone, so re-running the same template is safe (idempotent) and the file itself is the version-controlled source of truth. The imperative CLI script is the near-miss — it can also be stored in source control, but it describes steps, not a state, which is why a re-run collides with what already exists. Adding delete-then-create steps makes re-runs destructive rather than safe. A Read-only lock protects what was deployed but doesn't make deployment repeatable, and Advisor can suggest improvements but never deploys anything.

q: Which Azure tool would specifically flag that a company is paying for several unattached, unused disks?
opts: Microsoft Purview
Azure Service Health
Azure Policy, if configured to deny disk creation
Azure Advisor
why: Azure Advisor analyzes usage and cost, and will flag unused resources like orphaned disks as a cost-saving opportunity. A deny-effect Policy could stop new unattached disks from being created going forward, but it doesn't flag ones that already exist, and neither Purview nor Service Health looks at resource utilization at all.

q: A company wants to know immediately if there's an ongoing Azure platform outage affecting a region they use, separate from the health of their own individual resources. Which service fits?
opts: Microsoft Purview
Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor, using its resource health alerts
Azure Advisor
why: Service Health reports on the health of the Azure platform itself. Azure Monitor's resource health signal is about your own resource's connectivity to the platform, not whether Azure's infrastructure in that region is having a broader outage — a subtle but real distinction.

q: A web app in West Europe starts returning errors minutes after a deployment. Before rolling back, the on-call engineer wants to rule out a problem on Microsoft's side. Which tool answers whether the cause is a platform incident rather than their own release?
opts: Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor metrics for the App Service
Azure Advisor reliability recommendations
Microsoft Defender for Cloud's secure score
why: Service Health reports incidents, planned maintenance, and advisories affecting the Azure platform itself, filtered to the regions and services you use — the one place that says 'Microsoft has an active issue in West Europe.' Monitor metrics are the near-miss: they would confirm the error rate climbed, but they describe your resource's symptoms, not whether the platform underneath is at fault. Advisor offers longer-term design recommendations, not live incident status, and secure score measures security posture, which has nothing to do with an outage.

q: A finance team wants monthly spending broken down by department, using labels applied to each resource when it was created. Which feature enables this, combined with Cost Management?
opts: Management groups, since cost naturally rolls up by group
A separate subscription per department
Resource locks
Tags
why: Tags are name/value pairs applied directly to a resource and used to filter cost reports by whatever label you choose, like department. A separate subscription per department would also let you break down cost, but it's a much heavier restructuring than 'labels applied to each resource' calls for, and management groups organize subscriptions for governance, not cost tagging.

q: Which of these would Azure Policy be best suited to enforce?
opts: Automatically scale a VM Scale Set based on CPU usage
Notify the security team when a login occurs from a new country
Every new storage account must use only approved SKUs
Give a specific user permission to restart VMs but nothing else
why: The other three describe RBAC (a scoped permission grant), Conditional Access or an alert rule (a sign-in condition triggering a notification), and autoscaling respectively. Only the first is a standing configuration rule evaluated against resources — exactly what Azure Policy enforces.

q: A production resource group carries a Delete lock. An administrator who is an Owner on the subscription must urgently delete one VM inside that group. Which sequence is correct?
opts: Remove the lock, delete the VM, then re-apply the lock
Delete the VM directly, since Owner rights override the lock
Switch the lock to Read-only, which allows deletion but not edits
Wait for the lock to expire, since locks are time-limited
why: Locks apply regardless of RBAC role — even an Owner cannot delete through one — and a lock on a resource group is inherited by every resource inside it, so the VM is covered. The only path is to remove (or temporarily remove) the lock, perform the deletion, and put it back; Owner or User Access Administrator rights are what allow managing the lock itself. A Read-only lock is stricter, not looser: it blocks modification and deletion. Locks never expire on their own.

q: An architect wants one place to see health, performance, and log data across VMs, App Services, and databases, with the ability to configure alerts. Which service fits?
opts: Azure Advisor
Azure Monitor
Azure Service Health
Microsoft Purview
why: Azure Monitor is the unified telemetry, logging, and alerting service across your own resources. Service Health reports on the Azure platform rather than your workloads, Advisor gives point-in-time recommendations rather than ongoing telemetry, and Purview is focused on data governance, not resource health.

q: Which Azure Monitor component would you use to write a custom query against collected log data to find failed login attempts in the last 24 hours?
opts: Application Insights
Log Analytics
Azure Advisor
Azure Service Health
why: Log Analytics is the querying and storage layer within Azure Monitor for exactly this kind of custom log query. Application Insights is scoped to application performance telemetry specifically, and Advisor/Service Health don't support custom log querying at all.

q: A company is deploying identical infrastructure to Dev, Test, and Prod and wants a guarantee that all three are configured identically, with the deployment definition stored in source control. Which approach fits best?
opts: An Azure Policy that audits each environment for drift after deployment
Infrastructure as Code using ARM templates
Azure Advisor recommendations
A single shared resource lock across all three
why: IaC stored in source control is what guarantees identical, repeatable, trackable deployments across environments in the first place. An auditing policy could catch drift after the fact, but only once it's already happened — it doesn't guarantee the initial deployments matched, which is what this scenario asks for.

q: An Azure Policy blocks creation of any VM without a 'CostCenter' tag, and a developer's deployment fails as a result. What does this indicate about the policy's effect setting?
opts: It's using an Append effect, which adds the missing tag automatically
Policy cannot block deployments, only report on them
It's using an Audit-only effect, which only reports non-compliance
It's using a Deny effect
why: A Deny effect actively blocks non-compliant deployments — the deployment failing is the tell. Audit only reports non-compliance without stopping it, and Append would add the missing tag automatically rather than blocking the deployment outright, so neither matches what happened here.

q: A manager asks two questions: 'Exactly how much did the analytics team spend last month, by resource?' and 'Which of their VMs are oversized for their actual load?' Which tool answers each?
opts: Cost Management cost analysis for the spend; Azure Advisor for the oversized VMs
Azure Advisor for the spend; Cost Management cost analysis for the oversized VMs
The Pricing calculator for the spend; Cost Management cost analysis for the oversized VMs
Cost Management cost analysis for both, since it includes right-sizing recommendations
why: Cost analysis in Cost Management is the reporting tool for actual, historical spend, sliced by resource, tag, or time. Advisor is the tool that looks at utilization and recommends specific actions such as downsizing an underused VM. Swapping them fails because Advisor doesn't itemize invoices and cost analysis doesn't judge whether a VM is oversized. The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of resources you plan to deploy, not what you were actually billed, and cost analysis has no right-sizing logic of its own.

q: A subscription-level policy that denies resources outside East US can be overridden by assigning a more permissive allowed-locations policy at a resource group beneath it.
opts: True
False
why: Policy assignments accumulate down the hierarchy; they do not replace one another. A resource in that resource group is evaluated against both assignments, and the subscription-level Deny still blocks anything outside East US no matter what the lower-scope policy allows. A lower scope can only add restrictions, never loosen inherited ones — relaxing the rule for one group requires changing or exempting the higher assignment itself. The statement assumes 'closest scope wins,' which is how some systems work but not Azure Policy.

q: A Delete lock applied to a resource group blocks deletion of the group itself but still allows individual resources inside it to be deleted.
opts: True
False
why: Locks are inherited by everything beneath the scope they are applied to, so a Delete lock on a resource group protects the group and every resource in it — the most restrictive lock in the chain applies. That inheritance is what makes a group-level lock useful for protecting a whole production workload with one setting. The statement imagines the lock as attached only to the container object, which would leave its contents unprotected; a Delete lock does still allow modification, but not deletion at any level.

q: Azure Advisor can flag a single-instance virtual machine as a reliability risk, but it will not move that VM into an availability set or availability zone for you.
opts: True
False
why: Advisor is a recommendation engine: it analyzes configuration and usage and tells you what to change — a lone VM with no redundancy is a classic reliability finding — but it never alters resources. Acting on a finding is a separate step you take (or automate) yourself, which is also why Advisor recommendations tend to pile up unactioned in real subscriptions. The misconception on the other side would be expecting Advisor to remediate like a Policy remediation task or an Automation runbook; it does neither.

q: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the service you would use to scan an on-premises SQL Server and classify which columns contain credit-card numbers across a hybrid data estate.
opts: True
False
why: Discovering, scanning, and classifying sensitive data across hybrid and multi-cloud sources is Microsoft Purview's job — it builds a data map and applies classifications such as credit-card or national-ID patterns. Defender for Cloud is a security-posture and threat-protection tool: it can tell you a SQL server is misconfigured or under attack (and can reach on-premises servers through Azure Arc), but it is not the data-governance catalog that labels what each column contains. Both services touch 'security' and 'hybrid,' which is why the exam pairs them as distractors.

q: Redeploying an unchanged ARM template to a resource group that already matches it creates a second copy of each resource.
opts: True
False
why: ARM templates are declarative and idempotent: Resource Manager compares the template's desired state with what exists and makes only the changes needed, so redeploying an unchanged template results in no changes rather than duplicates. That property is the whole reason templates are safer to re-run than an imperative script of create commands, which would collide with existing resources. The statement describes how a naive script behaves and misapplies it to IaC.

q: Applying a CostCenter tag to a resource changes which subscription that resource's charges are billed to.
opts: True
False
why: Tags are metadata used to organize, filter, and report — in Cost Management you can group or filter spend by a tag such as CostCenter, which is exactly how chargeback reports are built. They never affect how a resource runs or where it is billed: charges always accrue to the subscription the resource lives in. Moving charges to a different subscription requires moving the resource itself. The statement confuses labeling spend for reporting with actually redirecting the invoice.

q: A governance team wants to stop any new storage account from allowing anonymous public blob access, and separately wants a report of existing VMs missing an Owner tag without blocking anyone. Which two statements about using Azure Policy are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: A Deny effect blocks creation of new accounts that allow public access but does not change existing ones
An Audit effect marks untagged VMs as non-compliant without stopping deployments
An Audit effect adds the missing Owner tag to each VM automatically
A Deny effect removes public access from accounts that already allow it
why: Deny is preventive: it rejects new or updated deployments that violate the rule, and existing violators are only reported as non-compliant. Audit is informational: it flags non-compliance on the compliance dashboard and never blocks or changes anything, which is what the team wants for the tag report. Adding a tag automatically is the Modify (or Append) effect, not Audit, and no effect retroactively reconfigures existing resources without a separate remediation task — so the two distractors each give an effect a power it does not have.

q: A Read-only lock is applied to a production resource group. Which three of the following operations will fail while it is in place? (Choose three.)
opts: Resizing a VM in the group
Viewing a VM's CPU metrics in the portal
Deleting a storage account in the group
Listing the resources the group contains
Creating a new VM in the group
why: A Read-only lock is inherited by everything in the group and blocks any operation that would change state — resizing (an update), deleting, and creating all fail, regardless of the user's RBAC role. Read operations are unaffected, so viewing metrics and listing resources still work. A common mistake is to assume a Read-only lock blocks nothing but edits to existing resources; creating a new resource inside the locked scope is a write to that scope and is blocked just the same.

q: A startup on the free Basic support plan, with no paid add-ons, wants to improve its environment without increasing spend. Which two capabilities are available to it at no additional charge? (Choose two.)
opts: Personalized Azure Advisor recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance
Azure Service Health alerts for platform incidents affecting its regions
Microsoft Defender for Cloud's enhanced workload protection plans
A committed one-hour response time from Microsoft for a production outage
An Azure Data Box device for moving data into Azure
why: Advisor and Service Health are included with every subscription at no cost — Advisor's recommendations and Service Health's incident alerts need nothing more than configuring them. The near-miss is Defender for Cloud: its foundational posture features are free, but the enhanced workload protection plans the option names are paid per resource. A committed response time for a production outage requires a paid support plan, since Basic covers only billing and subscription issues. Data Box is a physical appliance billed per order plus shipping.

q: An operations team sees disk latency spike on one of its VMs and, at the same time, hears rumours of a Microsoft outage in that region. Which two statements correctly describe which tool answers which question? (Choose two.)
opts: Azure Monitor metrics show the VM's own disk latency over time
Azure Service Health shows whether Microsoft has an active incident in that region
Azure Service Health shows per-VM disk latency so you can confirm the spike
Azure Monitor requires a paid plan before it collects any platform metrics
why: The split is 'my resource' versus 'the platform.' Monitor collects metrics and logs from your own resources, so the VM's disk latency lives there. Service Health reports incidents, maintenance, and advisories about Azure itself, filtered to your regions and services, so it answers the outage question. Service Health never shows a resource's performance counters, and basic platform metrics in Monitor are collected automatically at no charge — costs only come in for log ingestion and retention beyond the free amounts.

q: An Azure service's SLA guarantees 99.9% monthly uptime. Which statement correctly describes what that commitment actually means?
opts: The SLA applies only during the customer's local business hours, since that's when usage is highest
Microsoft commits to that uptime target and issues service credits if it isn't met, but some downtime can still occur
The customer is entitled to a full refund of that month's invoice the first time any downtime occurs
A 99.9% target is close enough to continuous uptime that Microsoft doesn't track or credit brief outages
why: An SLA is a measurable uptime commitment backed by service credits when missed — it is not a zero-downtime guarantee, and outages are tracked and credited according to the SLA terms regardless of how brief. The remedy is a partial, tiered credit rather than a full refund, and SLAs run continuously rather than only during business hours.

q: A web app depends on a web tier with a 99.95% SLA and a database tier with a 99.9% SLA, both of which must be up simultaneously for the app to work. What is true about the overall (composite) SLA?
opts: Composite SLA only applies to services deployed in the same Azure region
The composite SLA is fixed at exactly 99.9%, since that matches the lower component
The composite SLA is lower than either individual component's SLA, since both must be available at once
The composite SLA equals whichever individual SLA is higher
why: When dependent services must both be up, you multiply their uptime probabilities (0.9995 x 0.999 ≈ 99.85%), which lands below either individual figure — a scenario dependent on more sequential components generally has a LOWER overall SLA than any one piece. Composite SLA is a general math concept, not scoped to a region, and it isn't simply the higher or the lower value alone.

q: A startup on the free Basic Azure support plan needs a guaranteed fast response time from Microsoft when a production system goes down. What should they do?
opts: Nothing — Basic support already includes a committed response time for production-down issues
Purchase a Reserved Instance, which automatically upgrades support to Unified
Ask Azure Advisor to escalate the issue on their behalf
Upgrade to a paid support plan, such as Standard or Unified, which add committed response-time SLAs
why: Basic support is free and covers billing/subscription questions, but carries no response-time commitment for a production-down technical issue — that requires moving to a paid plan (Developer, Standard, Professional Direct, or Unified, the current name for what was formerly called Premier), where response-time commitments get faster at higher tiers. A Reserved Instance is a compute pricing commitment unrelated to support tier, and Advisor gives configuration recommendations, not support-ticket escalation.

q: A company owns on-premises Windows Server licenses with active Software Assurance. It will run Windows Server VMs in Azure around the clock for years and wants to cut the bill specifically by not paying Microsoft a second time for Windows. Which option targets that part of the cost?
opts: A three-year Reserved Instance
An Azure Savings Plan for compute
Azure Dev/Test pricing
Azure Hybrid Benefit
why: Azure Hybrid Benefit applies eligible existing Windows Server or SQL Server licenses to Azure VMs, removing the Windows licensing component from the hourly rate. A Reserved Instance and a Savings Plan are the near-misses: both are excellent for steady 24/7 usage, but they discount the underlying compute rate, not the license, and can be stacked with Hybrid Benefit rather than replacing it. Dev/Test pricing also removes Windows license charges, but only for non-production workloads under a Visual Studio subscription, which this long-running production fleet is not.

q: A 1-year Reservation and Spot pricing both discount Azure compute, but only Spot pricing carries the risk of the VM being evicted.
opts: True
False
why: A Reservation discounts a committed, predictable usage pattern with no eviction risk. Spot pricing discounts precisely because Azure can reclaim that capacity with little notice — a different trade-off entirely, even though both lower the bill versus pay-as-you-go.

q: Which two statements accurately describe Microsoft's approach to helping customers meet compliance requirements in Azure? (Choose two.)
opts: Achieving a certification like ISO 27001 for the Azure platform automatically certifies every customer's own workload built on it
Microsoft publishes independent audit reports and certifications, such as ISO 27001 and SOC 2, through resources like the Service Trust Portal
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager gives a compliance score and recommended actions for your own environment
Compliance becomes entirely Microsoft's responsibility once data is stored in Azure
why: Microsoft does publish independent audit reports/certifications and Compliance Manager does score and guide a customer's own compliance posture — but a platform-level certification doesn't automatically extend to a customer's own configuration and data, and compliance remains a shared responsibility, not Microsoft's alone.

q: A large enterprise wants to negotiate a direct, multi-year agreement with Microsoft covering a committed volume of Azure and other Microsoft products, rather than paying by credit card as usage occurs. Which Azure offer type fits?
opts: Pay-As-You-Go under a Microsoft Customer Agreement
An Enterprise Agreement (EA) / Microsoft Customer Agreement for enterprises
The Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program
A Visual Studio subscription with monthly Azure credits
why: An Enterprise Agreement (EA) — or its successor for enterprises, the Microsoft Customer Agreement for enterprises, as new EAs are being phased out — is a negotiated, direct, multi-year contract with Microsoft built around a committed volume of Azure and other Microsoft products, with centralized billing. Pay-As-You-Go under a Microsoft Customer Agreement is also a direct relationship, but it carries no upfront volume commitment and is billed as usage occurs — the model the enterprise is trying to move away from. CSP is the other near-miss: it is a real purchasing channel, but the agreement is with a Microsoft partner rather than negotiated directly with Microsoft. A Visual Studio subscription provides individual developer credits, not an organization-wide commercial agreement.

q: An Azure Cost Management budget, once its spending threshold is crossed, automatically blocks any further resource deployment in that scope.
opts: True
False
why: A budget by itself only triggers an alert notification when its threshold is crossed — it does not automatically stop deployments or spending. Actually preventing further spend requires pairing that alert with a separate automated action, like an Azure Policy or an Automation runbook that reacts to the alert, which is not something a budget does on its own.

q: A VM's monthly cost rose noticeably after a series of changes last month. Which two of those changes could explain the increase? (Choose two.)
opts: It was redeployed from one region to another with higher per-hour rates
It stopped being deallocated overnight and now runs around the clock
It was renamed to follow the new naming convention
A Department tag was added for chargeback reporting
It was moved to a different resource group in the same region
why: Region and consumption are two of the core factors that drive Azure cost: the same VM size is priced differently by region, and compute is billed for every hour the VM is allocated, so running 24/7 instead of office hours can roughly triple the compute charge. Names and tags are metadata with no effect on price, and a resource group is an organizational container — moving a VM between groups within the same region changes who manages it, not what it costs.

q: A finance team applied the tag CostCenter=Marketing to the Marketing resource group, yet cost analysis grouped by that tag still shows the group's VMs as untagged. What explains this?
opts: Resources do not inherit tags from their resource group unless a policy or script applies them
Tags on a resource group apply only to resources created after the tag was added
Cost analysis can group by subscription tags, but not by resource-level tags
A Delete lock on the VMs is blocking the tag from propagating
why: Tags are attached to the specific object they are placed on. Tagging a resource group tags the group itself; the VMs inside it keep whatever tags they individually carry, which here is none. To get consistent cost reporting you tag the resources themselves, typically enforced with an Azure Policy that inherits the group's tag onto new and existing resources. Creation time is irrelevant because inheritance isn't automatic in either direction; cost analysis groups by resource tags all the time; and a Delete lock only blocks deletion, not tagging.

q: A team sets a monthly Azure budget of $5,000 in Cost Management and configures an alert at 80% of that budget. Partway through the month, actual spend reaches $4,200. What happens next?
opts: Azure automatically stops all resources in the subscription once 80% of the budget is reached
An alert notification is sent, but resources keep running and spending is not blocked
The subscription is automatically downgraded to a free tier for the rest of the month
Azure Policy denies any further resource creation until the next billing cycle
why: A Cost Management budget alert is purely a notification — it tells the team spend has crossed a threshold, but it doesn't stop resources, downgrade the subscription, or block new deployments on its own. Actually enforcing a spending cap would require a separate action, like an Azure Policy or an Automation runbook triggered off that alert.

q: A security review produces two different lists of suggestions. One tool recommends resizing an oversized VM to cut cost, and separately flags a missing MFA requirement under its security recommendations. The other tool recommends enabling just-in-time VM access and patching a vulnerable container image, with no cost recommendations at all. Which tool produced which list?
opts: The first list came from Azure Advisor; the second came from Microsoft Defender for Cloud
The first list came from Microsoft Defender for Cloud; the second came from Azure Advisor
Both lists came from Azure Advisor, which covers cost and security together in one place
Both lists came from Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which also gives cost-saving recommendations
why: Advisor spans cost, reliability, performance, operational excellence, and security together — resizing for cost savings and an MFA gap are exactly the kind of two different pillars Advisor mixes into one recommendation list. Defender for Cloud is security-specific and wouldn't surface a cost recommendation at all — its list (just-in-time access, image vulnerabilities) has no cost content, which is the tell. The other two options either merge two genuinely separate tools into one, or hand Defender for Cloud a cost-recommendation role it doesn't have.

q: An administrator asks Copilot in Azure to draft an Azure CLI script that creates several storage accounts. Which approach matches Microsoft's guidance?
opts: Run the script immediately, because Copilot output is already validated and exempt from Azure Policy checks
Treat Copilot as an assistant: validate the recommendations, confirm permissions, and review the changes before applying them
Skip RBAC checks entirely, because Copilot acts with its own elevated permissions in the subscription
Avoid Cloud Shell altogether, because Copilot replaces the command-line tools
why: Copilot in Azure is an operational assistant, so you should still validate its suggestions, confirm permissions, and review deployment changes before applying them in production. Its output is not exempt from Azure Policy or from RBAC, and it does not replace Cloud Shell or the CLI.

q: A platform team worries that AI-assisted deployments could create resources in regions the company has banned. Which control keeps enforcing that standard regardless of how a change was proposed?
opts: Azure Service Health alerts for the affected regions
A cost budget alert at 80 percent of spend
An Azure Advisor reliability recommendation for each resource
An Azure Policy assignment that restricts allowed locations
why: Azure Policy enforces standards such as allowed locations, required tags, and approved SKUs no matter whether a person, Copilot, or automation proposed the change. Service Health reports platform issues, Advisor only recommends, and a budget alert notifies about spending without blocking deployments.

q: Which alert type notifies enterprise account owners when an Azure Prepayment balance reaches 90 percent and again at 100 percent?
opts: Budget alerts
Department spending quota alerts
Credit alerts
Service Health alerts
why: Credit alerts are generated automatically at 90 percent and 100 percent of the Azure credit balance for Prepayment, which is for Enterprise Agreement customers. Budget alerts fire on a threshold you set, department spending quota alerts relate to a department's fixed quota, and Service Health alerts are about platform events.

q: A team wants nonproduction resources shut down automatically when a monthly budget threshold is crossed. Which statement about Cost Management budgets is correct?
opts: Budgets are only available for Enterprise Agreement accounts and never for subscriptions
Budgets always stop all spending the moment the limit is reached, with no setup
Budgets can only send email notifications and cannot be connected to any automation at all
Budgets can be configured to trigger automation that suspends or modifies resources, in addition to sending notifications
why: Budgets notify through budget alerts and can also be configured to trigger automation, such as shutting down nonproduction resources, when a threshold is reached. They do not stop spending on their own, they are not limited to email, and they are not restricted to Enterprise Agreement accounts.

q: A company finds that moving 10 TB out of Azure from Europe to Asia costs more than moving it within Europe. Which concept best explains the pricing difference?
opts: Availability zones inside each region
Billing zones used for data-transfer pricing
The management group hierarchy
Region pairs used for recovery
why: Outbound data transfer is priced by billing zones, geographic groupings of regions used specifically for data-transfer pricing, so moving data across zones costs more than staying inside one. Availability zones are physically separate datacenters in a region, management groups organize subscriptions, and region pairs are a resiliency concept.

q: A governance team wants to track compliance against a regulatory goal that involves dozens of individual rules. Which Azure Policy construct groups those related definitions?
opts: A resource lock
A management group
A role assignment
A policy initiative
why: An initiative groups related policy definitions so their combined compliance state can be tracked against a larger goal. A resource lock prevents deletion or modification, a management group organizes subscriptions, and a role assignment grants identities permissions, so none groups policy definitions.

q: Before opening a support case, an engineer who is not signed in to any Azure account wants to know whether a widespread outage is affecting Azure as a whole. Which tool should they check?
opts: Resource Health for a specific VM
Azure Advisor
Azure status
A Log Analytics query
why: Azure status gives a global picture of Azure health across all services and regions and is the first place to look when a widespread outage is rumored. Resource Health describes one resource in your own subscription, Advisor gives configuration recommendations, and a Log Analytics query examines your own collected data rather than Azure-wide health.

q: The same on-call group should be emailed and paged by a metric alert, a Service Health alert, and an Advisor alert. What is the efficient way to do this?
opts: Create one reusable action group and reference it from all three
Create a separate action group for each alert and keep the lists in sync by hand
Use resource locks to route notifications
Tag each resource with the contact list
why: An action group controls who is notified and what happens next, and action groups are reusable across Azure Monitor, Service Health, and Azure Advisor alerts. Maintaining duplicates by hand creates drift, and locks and tags do not route notifications.

q: A low-traffic app is quiet at night, so nobody notices if it stops responding until morning. The team wants to know the moment it fails even with no real users. What should they configure?
opts: A read-only lock on the app
An Azure Advisor cost recommendation
Application Insights availability tests
Reserved capacity for the app
why: Availability tests send synthetic requests to the application so you learn it is down even during low-traffic periods. An Advisor cost recommendation is about spending, a read-only lock only prevents changes, and reserved capacity is a pricing commitment, so none of them detects an outage.

q: A company buys a managed backup solution from Azure Marketplace. How is it billed?
opts: Only the Azure services used are billed, and the vendor charges nothing beyond that usage
The Azure services used plus the vendor's charges, with the billing structure set by the vendor
A flat Microsoft fee that is set centrally by Azure Policy for all offers
The vendor's fee only, because the Azure resources behind a Marketplace offer are always free of charge
why: Marketplace purchases may include the cost of the Azure services in use plus the vendor's own services or expertise, and the vendor sets the billing structure. Offers are certified to comply with Azure policies and standards, but that does not make the vendor's fee or the Azure usage free.

q: Azure CLI is limited to read-only operations, so creating resources requires Azure PowerShell.
opts: True
False
why: Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are functionally equivalent; the main difference is syntax, with the CLI using Bash-style commands and PowerShell using cmdlets. Both can create, change, and delete resources and both are available in Cloud Shell and installable on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

q: Every document on the Service Trust Portal can be downloaded anonymously, with no sign-in or agreement.
opts: True
False
why: To access some Service Trust Portal resources you must sign in with a Microsoft Entra work or school account and accept the Microsoft nondisclosure agreement for compliance materials.

q: Which two resource types can Azure Arc manage when they run outside Azure? (Choose two.)
opts: Servers
Kubernetes clusters
Microsoft Entra tenants
Azure Policy definitions
why: Arc projects servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, SQL Server, and virtual machines (preview) into Azure Resource Manager. A Microsoft Entra tenant is an identity directory and a policy definition is an Azure governance object, neither of which is infrastructure hosted outside Azure.
